Overtake
o-ver-tāke´
v. (to come up with in pursuit; rendering Hebrew nasag, Greek katalambano)
A plain English compound, to take over or come upon from behind. Scripture uses it for blessings and curses alike — both pictured as things that pursue a man.

Biblical Definition

Overtake is a pursuit word, and Deuteronomy 28 puts it to unforgettable use on both sides of the covenant. Of obedience: “all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God” (Deu 28:2) — blessings chasing a man down, catching him from behind. Of disobedience, in identical form: “all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee” (Deu 28:15), and again, “shall pursue thee, and overtake thee, till thou be destroyed” (Deu 28:45). The same verb, the same posture, opposite contents. Pharaoh boasts it at the sea — “I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil” (Exo 15:9) — five confident first-person verbs, and the sea closes over every one. And David asks God whether pursuit is warranted, and is answered exactly: “Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all” (1Sa 30:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines overtake as to come up with in a course, pursuit or motion — and to come upon, to take by surprise, as calamity overtakes the sinner.

expand to see more

OVERTA´KE, v.t. To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch.

2. To come upon; to take by surprise.

Lest that day come upon you unawares. Luke xxi.

Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye who are spiritual, restore such a one. Gal. vi.

Key Scripture

Deu 28:2 — "And all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God."

Deu 28:15 — "But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:"

Exo 15:9 — "The enemy said, I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil; my lust shall be satisfied upon them; I will draw my sword, my hand shall destroy them."

1Sa 30:8 — "And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all."

Modern Corruption

Consequences imagined as escapable by distance or delay — when Deuteronomy pictures both blessing and curse as pursuers that do not tire.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 28's image is more searching than a simple statement of consequence. Blessings and curses do not merely follow from conduct; they pursue and overtake. A man may outrun them for a season, which is exactly why the delay deceives him, and the verb is chosen to say that the interval is not an escape. Nothing in modern life has changed the arithmetic; it has only lengthened the interval and multiplied the distractions inside it.

The pastoral use is the reverse and is often missed. Deuteronomy 28:2 says blessings overtake the obedient — they come from behind, unlooked-for, catching a man who was not calculating them. That forecloses the transactional reading of covenant obedience, in which a man performs and then collects. The blessings are described as pursuing him while he walks, which is a far better picture of the Christian life than a ledger. And Galatians 6:1 applies the same verb tenderly: a man overtaken in a fault is to be restored, not finished off.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nasag (H5381), to reach, overtake, attain — used of pursuers and of blessings; Greek katalambano (G2638), to seize, lay hold of — also Paul's word for apprehending the prize.

expand to see more

Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to overtake, reach, be able; blessings and curses alike overtake in Deu 28.

Greek katalambano (G2638) — to lay hold of, seize; the darkness comprehended it not (John 1:5), and Paul presses to apprehend that for which he was apprehended (Php 3:12).

Greek prolambano (G4301) — to take beforehand, overtake; if a man be overtaken in a fault (Gal 6:1).

Usage

"“All these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee” — blessings as pursuers."

"“Shall pursue thee, and overtake thee” — the interval is not an escape."

"“I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil” — and the sea closed over him."
